subject: ss-cardiology
title: Syncope: Risk Stratification and Diagnostic Evaluation

steps.tx: Syncope is defined as a **transient loss of consciousness** secondary to transient global **cerebral hypoperfusion**, characterized by rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery. Differentiating syncope from non-syncopal conditions including epileptic seizures, psychogenic pseudosyncope, and metabolic coma is essential. Comprehensive clinical evaluation requires careful correlation with serial electrocardiographic tracings and hemodynamic parameters.

rows: Benign long-term prognosis, zero excess mortality
Autonomic failure or intravascular volume depletion
Moderate risk, associated with cardiovascular disease
Structural heart disease or primary cardiac arrhythmia

steps.tx: **Vasovagal syncope** represents the most common form of **reflex syncope**, mediated by cardioinhibitory bradycardia, vasodepressor hypotension, or mixed responses. Emotional stress, severe pain, or prolonged standing in warm environments trigger paradoxical sympathetic withdrawal and profound vagal overactivity resulting in cerebral hypoperfusion. Comprehensive clinical evaluation requires careful correlation with serial electrocardiographic tracings and hemodynamic parameters.

Emotional stress, severe pain, or prolonged standing in warm environments trigger paradoxical sympathetic withdrawal and profound vagal overactivity resulting in cerebral hypoperfusion. left.title: Vasovagal Reflex Syncope
points: Triggered by fear, pain, instrumentation, prolonged standing
Prominent prodrome: diaphoresis, pallor, nausea, yawning
Rapid recovery upon adopting the supine posture
Zero structural cardiac pathology

right.title: Carotid Sinus Syndrome
points: Triggered by head turning, tight collar, shaving
Exaggerated response to carotid baroreceptor stimulation
Common in elderly males with vascular calcification
Evaluated via bedside carotid sinus massage

steps.tx: **Carotid sinus massage** is diagnostic when inducing **ventricular asystole** at least **3** seconds or a fall in systolic blood pressure at least **50** mmHg with reproduction of symptoms, contraindicated in patients with carotid bruits or prior stroke. Testing requires continuous electrocardiographic and blood pressure monitoring.
steps.say: Carotid sinus massage is diagnostic when inducing ventricular asystole at least 3 seconds or a fall in systolic blood pressure at least 50 mmHg with reproduction of symptoms, contraindicated in patients with carotid bruits or prior stroke. Testing requires continuous electrocardiographic and blood pressure monitoring.

left.title: Cardioinhibitory Response
points: Ventricular asystole duration >= 3 seconds
Driven by exaggerated vagal efferent discharge
Heart rate drops precipitously during massage
Responsive to dual-chamber permanent cardiac pacing

right.title: Vasodepressor Response
points: Systolic blood pressure drop >= 50 mmHg
Driven by reflex sympathetic withdrawal and vasodilation
Heart rate may remain unchanged during hypotension
Unresponsive to pacing; requires midodrine or fludrocortisone

steps.tx: **Orthostatic hypotension** is defined by a sustained drop in systolic BP at least **20** mmHg or diastolic BP at least **10** mmHg within **3** minutes of standing or **head-up tilt** testing, evaluating autonomic failure or volume depletion. Failure of heart rate to rise indicates neurogenic baroreflex failure.
steps.say: Orthostatic hypotension is defined by a sustained drop in systolic BP at least 20 mmHg or diastolic BP at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing or head-up tilt testing, evaluating autonomic failure or volume depletion. Failure of heart rate to rise indicates neurogenic baroreflex failure.

nodes.label: Measure Supine Blood Pressure and Heart Rate (5 min Rest)
Measure Standing BP and Heart Rate at 1 and 3 Minutes
Sustained SBP Drop >= 20 mmHg or DBP Drop >= 10 mmHg Confirms OH
Heart Rate Rise < 10 bpm Indicates Neurogenic Autonomic Failure

steps.tx: **Cardiac syncope** includes mechanical structural heart disease and primary arrhythmias, characterized by sudden loss of consciousness without prodrome, syncope in the supine position, or **syncope during exertion**. Exertional syncope strongly suggests critical aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, or inherited arrhythmogenic channelopathies. Comprehensive clinical evaluation requires careful correlation with serial electrocardiographic tracings and hemodynamic parameters.

left.title: High-Risk Cardiac Syncope
points: Occurs during active physical exertion
Occurs while supine or in bed
Sudden onset without warning autonomic prodrome
Associated with chest pain, palpitations, or known structural disease

right.title: Low-Risk Neurally Mediated Syncope
points: Occurs after standing for prolonged periods
Occurs post-micturition, post-cough, or post-defecation
Preceded by classic pallor, lightheadedness, nausea
Absence of personal or family structural heart disease

steps.tx: **Implantable loop recorders** provide continuous **subcutaneous ECG** monitoring for up to **3** to **4** years, representing the highest diagnostic yield test for recurrent unexplained syncope of suspected arrhythmic origin. Automatic activation algorithms capture bradycardic pauses, complete AV block, and ventricular tachycardias. Comprehensive clinical evaluation requires careful correlation with serial electrocardiographic tracings and hemodynamic parameters.

steps.tx: An **Electrophysiology study** in syncope evaluation is indicated in patients with previous MI or structural heart disease where non-invasive testing is non-diagnostic, assessing **HV interval** abnormal if at least **70** ms and VT inducibility. Significant infranodal prolongation warrants permanent pacing. Comprehensive clinical evaluation requires careful correlation with serial electrocardiographic tracings and hemodynamic parameters.

rows: Baseline HV interval ≥  70 ms (or block with pacing)
Sustained VT induced with programmed stimulation
Corrected SNRT > 525 ms or SACT > 140 ms
No inducible arrhythmia and normal HV interval

steps.tx: Pharmacotherapy for refractory neurogenic orthostatic hypotension includes **Midodrine**, a selective alpha-**1** adrenergic agonist, and **fludrocortisone**, a synthetic mineralocorticoid promoting renal sodium retention and plasma volume expansion. Non-pharmacologic physical counter-maneuvers, adequate hydration, salt supplementation, and abdominal binders form the essential therapeutic foundation.

left.title: Midodrine (Alpha-1 Agonist)
points: Direct arteriolar and venous vasoconstriction
Increases systemic vascular resistance and venous return
Dosed 2.5 to 10 mg three times daily before upright activity
Avoid dosing within 4 hours of bedtime to prevent supine hypertension

right.title: Fludrocortisone (Mineralocorticoid)
points: Enhances renal distal tubular sodium and water reabsorption
Sensitizes vascular alpha-adrenergic receptors
Dosed 0.1 to 0.2 mg daily with dietary sodium supplementation
Requires monitoring for hypokalemia and peripheral edema
